statement: In healthy young men in a sleep laboratory, morning caffeine after a bedtime benzodiazepine sleeping pill (triazolam or flurazepam), compared with a morning placebo after the same pill, was followed by less sleepiness on four sleepiness measures taken together, although on the nap test alone the difference was clear only after the higher flurazepam dose; performance on reaction-time, memory and other tests, and mood, did not differ significantly, in one small randomized double-blind trial with ten men per group (Johnson et al., 1990). The trial did not test driving, lasted two nights, excluded heavy caffeine consumers and kept everyone off caffeine in the laboratory; evidence is insufficient to say whether caffeine undoes the next-day effects of a sleeping pill. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small lab study, caffeine in the morning made young men less sleepy after a sleeping pill, but their test scores were not clearly better.
population: 80 healthy young men (mean age 20), good sleepers with a low usual caffeine intake (threshold on the study card), in a naval sleep laboratory (ten per group)
exposure: Caffeine early in the morning after a bedtime benzodiazepine sleeping pill (triazolam or flurazepam), on two days (study amounts and times on the study card)
comparator: A morning placebo after the same bedtime pill (and, for comparison, caffeine or placebo after a bedtime placebo)
outcome: Next-day objective sleepiness (Multiple Sleep Latency Test), lapses, self-rated sleepiness, performance tests and mood
magnitude: Mean MSLT sleep latency over two days: triazolam (higher dose) 7.61 min with morning placebo against 12.60 with caffeine; flurazepam (higher dose) 5.47 against 9.62; editors' calculation d about 1.1 and 1.0; caffeine groups significantly more alert on the morning trials, not significantly by early afternoon (P = 0.064 and 0.063). Performance: treatment trend only, F(7,65) = 1.98, P < 0.07; mood: no significant group effect.

evidence.extracted: Mean MSLT sleep latency: higher-dose triazolam with morning placebo 7.61 (SD 3.79) min against 12.60 (SD 5.12) with caffeine; higher-dose flurazepam 5.47 (SD 3.06) against 9.62 (SD 4.66); placebo night 6.32 (SD 2.54) against 10.73 (SD 3.74); editors' calculation: differences of 5.0, 4.2 and 4.4 min.

evidence.extracted: No significant group effects on individual performance tests, although trial-by-group interactions were significant for digit-symbol substitution and reaction time; pairwise digit-symbol differences: on day 1 caffeine after a placebo night beat placebo-placebo, and on day 2 higher-dose flurazepam with morning placebo scored below lower-dose flurazepam, higher-dose flurazepam with caffeine and lower-dose triazolam; no significant group effects on mood (POMS or visual analogue mood).

risk_of_bias.note: Randomization method not described, pairs treated alike but analysed as individuals, baseline MSLT imbalance, an outlier excluded (card overall: some concerns).

indirectness.note: Healthy young men and good sleepers kept off caffeine for two days, two nights of treatment, no driving outcome; people who take sleeping pills for insomnia and drink caffeine daily were not studied.

imprecision.note: Ten men per group; the performance and mood results cannot exclude a benefit or no benefit.

grade.reasoning: A randomized double-blind trial starts high; downgraded for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low. The relation is insufficient evidence because the question people ask (does morning caffeine undo the effects of a sleeping pill, for example for driving) was not answered: sleepiness on a nap test fell, while performance did not detectably improve. The claim covers two drugs because the trial studied their combination; caffeine's effect in men who had been kept off caffeine may partly reflect relief of mild withdrawal.
